theme: The gospel; the righteousness of God; the wrath of God
readingInstruction: Read Romans 1:1-32. This is the opening of Paul’s greatest letter. Read the greeting (1:1-7), then the theme statement (1:16-17), and then the dark diagnosis of the human race (1:18-32). Ask what makes the gospel good news, and why it must begin with bad news.
settingTheScene: Paul writes to the church in Rome from Corinth, around AD 57, at the end of his third missionary journey. He has never been to Rome, but he hopes to visit on his way to Spain. The church is made up of Jewish and Gentile believers who have tensions between them. Paul writes the fullest explanation of the gospel found anywhere in Scripture: how sinners are made right with a holy God, how they are changed, and how God’s promises to Israel and the nations fit together. Romans is the great explanation of the new covenant. The Reformation was lit by it, and countless believers have been converted while reading it.
observation: “Paul, a servant of Christ Jesus, called to be an apostle, set apart for the gospel of God” (1:1).
“And was declared to be the Son of God in power according to the Spirit of holiness by his resurrection from the dead, Jesus Christ our Lord” (1:4).
“For I am not ashamed of the gospel, for it is the power of God for salvation to everyone who believes, to the Jew first and also to the Greek” (1:16).
“For in it the righteousness of God is revealed from faith for faith, as it is written, The righteous shall live by faith” (1:17).
“For the wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all ungodliness and unrighteousness of men, who by their unrighteousness suppress the truth” (1:18).
“For his invisible attributes, namely, his eternal power and divine nature, have been clearly perceived, ever since the creation of the world, in the things that have been made” (1:20).
“For although they knew God, they did not honor him as God or give thanks to him” (1:21).
“Because they exchanged the truth about God for a lie and worshiped and served the creature rather than the Creator, who is blessed forever! Amen” (1:25).
interpretation:
Paul introduces himself as a servant, literally a slave, of Christ Jesus, an apostle, set apart for the gospel of God. He immediately says that this gospel was promised beforehand through the prophets in the holy Scriptures. The good news is not new. It is the fulfillment of the Old Testament. Its subject is God’s Son, descended from David according to the flesh and declared to be the Son of God in power by his resurrection from the dead. Through him, Paul has received grace and apostleship “to bring about the obedience of faith for the sake of his name among all the nations.” He writes to Romans who are “called to be saints.” Every Christian is a saint, a holy one set apart by God.

Paul longs to see them, to impart some spiritual gift, and to be mutually encouraged. Then he gives the thesis of the whole letter: “I am not ashamed of the gospel, for it is the power of God for salvation to everyone who believes, to the Jew first and also to the Greek.” The gospel is not advice; it is power. It saves. And it saves “everyone who believes,” on one condition. Verse 17 states the heart: “In it the righteousness of God is revealed from faith for faith, as it is written, The righteous shall live by faith.” This is a quotation of Habakkuk 2:4. The righteousness of God here is God’s saving action and the gift of righteous standing that he gives. Martin Luther said that when he understood this phrase he felt he had entered paradise through open gates.

But why do we need the gospel? Paul now tells the bad news. “The wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all ungodliness and unrighteousness of men, who by their unrighteousness suppress the truth.” People know God from creation: his eternal power and divine nature are clearly perceived in the things he has made. So no one has an excuse. The problem is not lack of information but suppression of it. They knew God, but they did not honor him as God or give thanks. Their thinking became futile, their hearts darkened. Claiming to be wise, they became fools, exchanging the glory of the immortal God for images. Three times, Paul says, “God gave them up”: to impurity, to dishonorable passions, to a debased mind. God’s judgment here takes the form of letting sin run its course. The chapter ends with a long list of sins and the sober note that they not only do these things but give approval to those who practice them.

This is hard reading. But it prepares the way. A doctor who diagnoses cancer gently cannot be trusted. Paul tells the truth so that the good news may be heard as good.
connection: Habakkuk 2:4 is the source of 1:17. Psalm 19:1-4 declares that the heavens proclaim God’s glory. Genesis 1 to 3 is the background for the fall in 1:21-25. Acts 14:15-17 and 17:22-31 show Paul preaching the same truth about creation. Jeremiah 2:11-13 describes exchanging glory for what cannot profit. Ephesians 4:17-19 describes darkened understanding. 1 Corinthians 1:18-25 speaks of the power of the cross. Romans 3:21 to 5:21 will answer the problem posed here.
application:
Memorize Romans 1:16 and ask whether you are ashamed of the gospel in any setting. Where are you tempted to stay silent?

Ask what you honor above God or give thanks for in a way that forgets the Giver.

Thank God that he does not leave us at the end of Romans 1.
prayerPrompts: Thank God for the gospel, the power for salvation.
Ask him to keep you from shame in it.
Thank him that the righteous shall live by faith.
